set.text: By the time Priya reached the night market, she was famished; she had skipped lunch to finish a report. The long rows of stalls offered a cornucopia of choices: grilled corn, steamed buns, spicy noodles, mango sticky rice and a dozen kinds of soup. Her friend Tomás, a finicky eater who picks the onions out of everything, walked past six stalls before he found one he trusted. Priya was far less fussy. She bought a skewer of grilled chicken and ate every morsel before Tomás had even ordered. The mood around the shared tables was convivial. Strangers passed sauces to one another, a family let the two friends squeeze onto their bench, and an old man explained which dumplings were worth the wait. An hour later, Priya leaned back with a happy sigh. Nothing, she said, could sate a hunger quite like food eaten outdoors with good company.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “finicky” mean?
options: very hard to please, especially about food
happy to try any new food
unable to eat certain foods for health reasons
slow and polite at the table
qs.why: Tomás picks onions out of everything and passes six stalls before choosing, so he is hard to please. Nothing in the passage says he has a health problem.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “convivial” mean?
qs.why: Strangers share sauces, make room on a bench and give advice, which shows a friendly, cheerful mood. The tables were shared, but they are not described as uncomfortable.

qs.q: Why did Priya finish eating before Tomás had ordered?
options: She was very hungry and chose quickly, while he took a long time to pick a stall.
Tomás had already eaten lunch and was not hungry.
The stall Tomás wanted was closed.
Priya wanted to leave the market early.
Tomás was waiting for a family to join them.
Priya's food was ready before anyone else's because it was cheaper.
qs.why: Priya had skipped lunch and was 'less careful,' while Tomás walked past six stalls before ordering.

why: 'Less careful' contrasted Priya with finicky Tomás, but finicky means hard to please, not careful; changed to 'far less fussy'.

set.text: A company once claimed that its copper bracelet could cure back pain, improve sleep and sharpen memory. The ads used phrases like 'energy fields' but offered no real tests. Dr. Aiko Tanaka, a researcher who studies treatments for pain, decided to look closer. She is no alarmist; she does not believe every new product is dangerous. But she knows that pseudoscience often hides behind scientific-sounding language. The company's main argument was specious: thousands of customers felt better, so the bracelet must work. Tanaka pointed out that many people with back pain improve over time anyway. Her team gave some volunteers the real bracelet and others a look-alike made of a different metal, without telling them which was which. Tanaka judged the results in a dispassionate way, looking at numbers, not stories. Both groups reported the same small gains. That was not incontrovertible proof that the bracelet could never help anyone, Tanaka said, but it gave no sign that it was efficacious.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “specious” mean?
options: sounding reasonable at first but actually misleading
qs.why: The argument sounds sensible, but Tanaka shows it is misleading because people with back pain often get better anyway.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “alarmist” mean?
options: a person who installs alarm systems
a person who sells health products
a person who never trusts science
a person who makes dangers seem much worse than they are
a person who enjoys taking risks
qs.why: The next words explain it: she does not believe every new product is dangerous, so she does not exaggerate danger.

qs.q: What did Tanaka's test show?
options: The bracelet cured back pain for most volunteers.
The look-alike bracelet caused more pain.
The bracelet was proven to be dangerous.
People wearing the real bracelet did no better than those wearing a look-alike.
Customers had lied about feeling better.
The bracelet helped with sleep but not pain.
qs.why: Both groups reported the same small gains, so the copper bracelet showed no extra effect. Tanaka did not say it was dangerous.

why: 'Dispassionate' (not swayed by emotion, judging fairly) describes a person or judgment, not numbers; rewrote so Tanaka judges dispassionately. 'Plain metal' was confusing since copper is itself a plain metal.

set.text: Farah Nasser has taught middle school science for twenty years, and she has seen every prank. This year, two boys hid a rubber snake inside a volcano model at the science fair. When a parent screamed, the boys laughed so hard they nearly fell off their chairs. It was asinine, but Ms. Nasser did not chastise them in front of the crowd. Instead, she took them aside after the event. She told them she knew they were callow, not cruel, but that the parent had been truly frightened. Her admonition was short and firm: 'Fun is fine. Scaring people is not.' The boys apologized sheepishly to the parent, staring at their shoes. One of them, Jake, is known as incorrigible; he has pulled a prank every month since September. But even he offered to help clean up the gym afterward.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “chastise” mean?
qs.why: She chose not to scold them harshly in public and instead spoke to them privately.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “incorrigible” mean?
options: having bad habits that seem impossible to change
qs.why: Jake has pulled a prank every month, so his habit seems impossible to correct.

qs.q: How did Ms. Nasser handle the prank?
options: She punished them in front of everyone.
She called their parents to the gym.
She spoke to the boys privately and firmly instead of scolding them in public.
She laughed and joined the joke.
She cancelled the rest of the science fair.
qs.why: She 'did not chastise them in front of the crowd' but took them aside and gave a short, firm warning.

why: 'Puerile' is defined as childish in a way inappropriate for an adult; applied to middle-school boys (who are children) it misuses the card meaning. Swapped in unused level word 'asinine'.

set.text: It began with a tiny hole in a bag of rice. Then Mei Lin found crumbs on the counter and heard something scurry behind the fridge at night. Mice had found their way into her apartment. A pest expert explained that mice scavenge for almost any food people leave behind, from crumbs and spilled cereal to scraps in the trash, and that two or three can quickly become dozens. Left alone, they can infest an entire building. They also gnaw on wires and wood, which can cause real damage. Mei Lin spent a Saturday sealing gaps with steel wool and putting food in glass jars. That night she crept stealthily into the kitchen with a flashlight to check her work. Nothing moved. A week later, she rummaged through the back of every cupboard, pushing boxes and cans aside to be sure, but she found no new signs. The visitors were gone.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “scavenge” mean?
options: search for food that others have left or thrown away
qs.why: Mice search for food that people leave behind or throw away, such as crumbs, spilled cereal and scraps in the trash.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “rummage” mean?
options: search by moving things around quickly and carelessly
qs.why: She pushed boxes and cans aside in the backs of cupboards to look for signs of mice.

qs.q: Why does the expert say mice should be dealt with quickly?
options: Mice are dangerous to adults who touch them.
Mice eat only rice and grain.
Steel wool makes mice more aggressive.
Mice usually leave on their own after a week.
A few mice can soon become many and damage a building.
qs.why: The expert says two or three mice can become dozens, can infest a building and gnaw wires and wood.

why: 'Scavenge' card = search through what others have thrown away; the text used it for cereal/pet food (stored food), which did not match the keyed option 'food others have left or thrown away'. Also made 'rummage' show moving things around, matching its card.

set.text: Every November, the fishing town of Port Ellery holds a concert to remember sailors lost at sea. It begins with the knell of the old church bell, one slow stroke for each name read aloud. Then the town band plays a dirge, so slow and heavy that even small children stand still. The middle of the program is elegiac but gentle, as a local choir sings old songs about boats that never came home. Thomas Breen, a folk-music aficionado who has recorded the town's songs for forty years, says the final piece is his favorite. It is a paean to the sea itself, praising its beauty and power, sung by the whole crowd. Its tune is so melodious that visitors often hum it for days. 'We are sad,' he explains, 'but we are also grateful.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “paean” mean?
options: a prayer for safety at sea
a song about pain and loss
qs.why: The passage explains that the song is 'praising its beauty and power.' The slow funeral song is the dirge, a different piece.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “aficionado” mean?
options: a person who knows a lot about something and loves it
a critic who dislikes folk music
the leader of the town band
a beginner who is just learning
qs.why: Thomas has recorded the town's songs for forty years, showing deep knowledge and enthusiasm.

qs.q: How does the mood of the concert change from beginning to end?
options: It moves from joy to anger.
It stays cheerful from start to finish.
It moves from quiet calm to fear.
It begins with praise and ends with a funeral song.
It moves from deep sorrow toward praise and gratitude.
qs.why: It opens with a bell and a dirge, and ends with a song of praise; Thomas says, 'We are sad, but we are also grateful.'

why: 'A single knell ... one stroke for each name' was self-contradictory (single vs many strokes).

set.text: Restaurant critic Elena Petrova believes in honest reviews, but she draws a line. A trenchant review, she says, points clearly to what failed: the soup was cold, the fish was dry, the service was slow. A vitriolic one is different; it attacks people, not food, and its goal is to hurt. Early in her career, Elena wrote a long diatribe about a small café, mocking the owner's taste in furniture and even his accent. Readers loved it, but she felt ashamed when she met the owner months later. Now she refuses to disparage chefs as people. She also avoids the backhanded compliment, such as 'the dessert was surprisingly good for a place like this.' And she has no patience for derisive comments from readers. 'You can say a meal was bad,' she says, 'without saying the cook is worthless.'

qs.q: In the passage, what does “trenchant” mean?
options: sharp, clear and forceful in criticism
qs.why: A trenchant review 'points clearly to what failed.' Cruel, personal attacks are what Elena calls vitriolic.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “backhanded” mean?
options: seeming like praise but really hiding an insult
qs.why: 'Surprisingly good for a place like this' sounds kind but insults the restaurant.

qs.q: Why did Elena change the way she writes about chefs?
options: Readers complained about her early reviews.
Her editor told her to be kinder.
She felt ashamed after meeting the owner of a café she had mocked.
She stopped eating at small cafés.
A chef took her to court.
She decided that honest reviews are unfair.
qs.why: After mocking a café owner in an early diatribe, she felt ashamed when she met him, and now she refuses to disparage chefs as people. Readers did not complain; they loved the review.

why: The idea question only restated the definitions of 'trenchant' and 'vitriolic' (already tested by a word question), which the brief forbids; replaced with an inference question about why Elena changed.

set.text: When Kenji Watanabe came home from a hiking trip with a fever, he thought it was just a cold. Instead, the malady lasted for weeks. The virus that afflicted him left him so weak that even climbing the stairs was hard. For a month, tiredness would incapacitate him by mid-afternoon, and he had to leave work early or stay home. His face looked pallid, and friends who visited noticed how listless he seemed, staring at the television without really watching it. His doctor explained that recovery would take time, but that some steps could ameliorate his symptoms: plenty of water, short walks, regular sleep and a slow return to normal activity. Kenji followed the plan. By the third month he was walking a mile each morning, and the color had come back to his cheeks.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “pallid” mean?
qs.why: Later 'the color had come back to his cheeks,' which shows his face had been pale.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “ameliorate” mean?
options: make better or easier to bear
qs.why: The steps could make his symptoms easier to live with. The doctor said recovery would take time, so they were not a complete cure.

qs.q: What best describes Kenji's recovery?
options: It happened overnight after he took medicine.
Going back to hiking cured him at once.
It was slow and gradual, helped by steady daily habits.
Staying in bed all day made him recover fastest.
qs.why: Recovery took months and came through water, short walks, sleep and a slow return to activity.

why: 'The virus that had come to afflict him' was awkward, unnatural phrasing.

set.text: Detective Nadia Brooks had been watching the jewelry shop for three nights. Each evening, the same man would loiter near the bus stop across the street, never catching a bus. His glances toward the shop's back door were quick and furtive, as if he feared being seen. On the fourth night, Nadia sat on a bench close enough to eavesdrop on his phone call. 'Not yet,' he said quietly. 'The alarm is still on.' The next morning, she brought him in for questioning. He was cagey, giving short answers and claiming he simply liked the quiet street. Nadia watched him warily; she knew one wrong move could warn his partners. Then she placed a small object on the table: a key to the shop, found in his coat. His face went white. The key alone did not prove he had planned a crime, but together with the phone call, it was beginning to incriminate him.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “furtive” mean?
options: secret and nervous, trying not to be noticed
qs.why: His glances were quick, 'as if he feared being seen,' which is secret, nervous behavior.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cagey” mean?
qs.why: He gave short answers and a weak excuse, avoiding saying what he really knew. 'Trapped' is a careless link to the word 'cage.'

qs.q: What can we conclude about the case at the end?
options: The man confessed to planning a robbery.
The key proved the man was innocent.
The shop was robbed that night.
Nadia let the man go for good.
Nadia had a useful clue but still needed more proof.
His partners had already been arrested.
qs.why: The key 'alone did not prove he had planned a crime,' though with the phone call it was beginning to make him look guilty, so more proof was needed.

why: 'Not enough to incriminate him' misused the card meaning (make someone seem guilty): a shop key in his coat does make him seem guilty. Rewrote so the evidence begins to incriminate him but does not yet prove the crime; updated idea 'why'.
